title: Ang 269–296: Sukhmani continues
tomorrow: is there a lucky day for a driving test?

lines: A SUKHMANI PATH BEFORE THE TEST?
cards: Some people have lucky socks for game day; some have a playlist before an exam. Bebe Jaswant has a suggestion for Simran's driving test, three days away: a Sukhmani path, the whole psalm read through, the morning of.
Simran's question is honest. So is that like a lucky charm? Maya, on the phone, says yes, basically.
Bebe says no, beta, it's not a charm. Sikhs have thought hard about this one, and there are two good answers.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: BRING YOUR WORRY WITH YOU.
teach.b: The first view: yes, read it, and bring your worry with you. Some Sikh families read the Sukhmani for a new home, an illness, an exam, a journey.
The psalm says it rests in the minds of devotees and brings peace, and Gurbani is full of people calling out in need.
On this view, reading it before a test isn't superstition. It's bringing your whole life, test included, to the Guru. The second view: careful.
The Guru's words aren't a charm that makes the result come out right. The Sukhmani's peace is for the mind, not for the score.
In the stretch we're reading, Ang 269 to 296, Guru Arjan describes the God-conscious person, in paraphrase: always untouched, like a lotus in water. The lotus doesn't stop the water rising.

teach.h: A BETTER DAY, OR A STEADIER YOU?
teach.b: It stays clean in it. On this view, you read to become the lotus, not to change the weather. Hear what each side is protecting.
The first protects honesty: you're allowed to need things.

The second protects the Word: it isn't a tool for getting them. Both read the same psalm, and both say the reading matters. They differ on what to expect from it: a better day, or a steadier you inside the day.

how: Sikhs read the Sukhmani daily or for a particular need, alone or as a family, sometimes at a gurdwara; readers differ on how to hold a reading done with a purpose in mind.

o: the page where the Sukhmani runs on past its opening
a page of the Sukhmani read only at funerals
the page where the Sukhmani ends and a new poem begins

games.q: two views of one psalm — tap the pairs.
p: bring your worry to the Guru
the Word is not a charm

s: Sikhs treat the Sukhmani as a charm that guarantees results
readers differ on what to expect, but its peace is for the mind, not a guaranteed score.
the Sukhmani pictures the God-conscious person as a lotus in water
untouched by the water, not keeping it away.

games.q: you side with Bebe. what's the strongest case for the other view, that the reading isn't for the result?
o: the psalm's peace is for the mind: you read to be the lotus, not to stop the water.
the Sukhmani is far too long to finish before a test anyway.
Gurbani never mentions anyone asking for help, so asking is wrong.
games.why: the best case for view two is the lotus: untouched in the water, not keeping the water away. both views read the same psalm, and neither treats it as luck.

practice: Close your eyes and let one worry come up, whatever's nearest: a test, a talk, a bill. Don't push it away; picture it as water, and yourself as a lotus resting on top of it, untouched.
Breathe, and let the water rise and fall without you sinking.

wordCard.voice: Ang 269: where the Sukhmani runs on, through the lotus in water, toward its last stanzas on Ang 296.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Sukhmani, the psalm of peace; it names itself in its rahao on Ang 262.

carryVoice: Your line: peace continues. Read it in need if you like, but read to become the lotus. Take care.
